name: West Futuna
catalog_citation: Dougherty, Janet W. D. 1983. West Futuna-Aniwa: An Introduction to a Polynesian Outlier Language. University of California Publications in Linguistics 102. Berkeley: University of California Press.
catalog_locator: Dougherty 1983, Phonology, pp. 12-14 (stress paragraph begins bottom of p.12; rule, examples and exceptions statement p.13; exceptions list top of p.14). Page …
catalog_quote: Stress can be assigned for the majority of West Futuna words by a rule that places primary stress of the final syllable if it is a vowel dipthong and otherwise on either the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable depending upon the stem shape. The general rule for stress assignment is: V → V́ / __ [-syl]₀ V·(V) (Dougherty 1978) The raised dot indicates a syllable boundary. The subscript indicates that the number of nonsyllablic units which follow the stressed vowel is not specified. None, one or two such phones are attested in West Futuna speech. Examples include: /ké/ different, strange /úa/ rain /pái/ far /fíe/ firewood /úri/ dark /mága/ to branch /úta/ a load, cargo /utáina/ to load something /síko/ ... /sikófia/ ... /fesáo(a)/ to speak, to tell something /ámo(a)/ to take or carry something /hkánu/ stripe /arátu/ tomorrow /méntua/ to think or remember /móega/ clothing /amósia/ t…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage, rule, example list and exceptions are verbatim on the held page images of Dougherty 1983 pp.12-14 at exactly the stated locator. (2) Deciding source: a 1983 reference grammar by the principal fieldworker, Glottolog's only full grammar for futu1245; nothing later or more specialised appears in Glottolog's descriptive list, and the two other primary stress statements that exist (Dougherty 1977 JPS, the source of the rule; Capell 1984 PL C-56 section 1.1.3.1) were fetched sources now from open copies and read. Both agree with the record: default penult, antepenult on consonant+ia/ua-final (transitive -ia) words, stress on the first vowel of a word-final falling diphthong, and a lexically marked final-stress class from historical long vowels. Capell refines rather than contradicts: he analyses final diphthongs as two-vowel clusters with stress on the penultimat

sources.quote: 'the statistically commonest type is the penultimate. There are more exceptions to the pattern in Aniwa than in Futuna because Aniwa often rejects final syllables that are present in Futuna ... in some cases there seems to be a free variation ... both /fa'nua/ and /'fanua/ 'land' will be met with. Final stress is more usual in Aniwa than in Futuna. Antepenultimate stress is found in some words in both languages. Many of the examples are provided by the transitive form of the verb ending in -ia preceded by a consonant. In these the stress does not necessarily move forward with the addition of a

sources.note: Only other modern primary description with a stress section (1.1.3.1, pp.8-9); independent fieldworker; adds Futuna-vs-Aniwa differences and free variation (fánua ~ fanúa, túkua ~ tukúa) not in our record; treats final diphthongs as vowel clusters stressed on the penultimate vowel, which bears on the weight-vs-mora reading behind our QS-HEDGED code.
